Drainage
Mine drainage systems must be designed to handle storm runoff and ground water which may accumulate in the mine cuts. Pumping may, under certain conditions, be necessary to prevent the ground water seepage from remaining in contact with exposed coal or waste and thus dissolving undersirable chemicals.
Mine drainage would not be allowed to flow directly into major watercourses in the drainage basins because it could carry chemical contamination and most certainly would carry sediment from the unconsolidated fill, particularly after storms. This water would be retained in holding basins for natural clarification and possible chemical treatment.
On Tract III, Westmoreland has constructed a dam and settling pond a few hundred yards north of the railroad loop. This impoundment handles runoff water from the existing mine area. There is no ground water flowing into the pits in the existing operation. Most of Tract III is on a low ridge which divides Sarpy Creek from East Fork Sarpy Creek. Mining in either tract would not enter the floodplains of these streams, and consequently no dams or diversions of these creeks would be required. Siltation dams will be required on several minor tributary drainages on the tract to prevent the direct flow of water into the above-mentioned creeks. Diversion ditches would be needed in some areas to intercept runoff in minor drainages and carry it to a settling pond. The middle fork of Sarpy Creek although intermittent within the lease boundaries, is the major drainage transecting the tract, and fairly substantial impoundments might be necessary on this drainage.
